R004.fact: For every natural n, the real coordinate space Ambient n with its given Euclidean inner product and norm is a finite-dimensional real normed vector space. Its coordinate vectors e_j, j∈Fin n, form a basis, including the empty basis for n=0; its metric also supplies an extended metric.

grounds.reason: n is a natural number, including zero, so Fin n is finite.
Ambient n is the real coordinate space with coordinatewise vector operations and its Euclidean inner product/norm.

R004.justification: Define e_j to have coordinate 1 at j and 0 elsewhere. Each x equals the finite sum Σ_j x_j e_j by evaluation at each coordinate. If Σ_j a_j e_j=0, evaluation at j gives a_j=0, proving independence. For n=0 every vector is the unique empty tuple, and spanning and independence hold for the empty family. Hence the space is finite dimensional. The supplied Euclidean inner product induces the displayed norm and the compatible real normed-space structure. Regard each finite real distance as an extended nonnegative distance to obtain the extended metric, preserving the metric axioms.

R005.fact: The real numbers with norm |x| and their usual addition and real scalar multiplication form a finite-dimensional real normed vector space, of dimension one, with basis consisting of 1.

grounds.reason: S001 explicitly takes the ambient space to be ℝ, with the standard real normed-space interpretation.
The supplied M012 statement requires the ambient real normed space to be finite dimensional; the present routine verification supplies precisely this condition for ℝ.

R005.justification: The real field operations give the real vector-space and additive-group laws. Absolute value is nonnegative, vanishes exactly at zero, is subadditive, and satisfies |a x|=|a||x|, so it gives the stated compatible norm. Every real x equals x·1, and a·1=0 implies a=0. Thus the singleton 1 spans and is linearly independent, proving finite dimensionality.

R101.fact: For the D004 infimum, enlarging the allowed scale decreases Content. Its supremum over positive extended scales equals its supremum over scales ofReal δ with real δ>0.

R101.justification: Every cover allowed at a smaller scale is allowed at a larger scale, so the larger-scale infimum is no greater. Each positive real scale occurs among the extended scales. R102.fact: For u>0, the map d -> d^u is increasing on extended nonnegative reals. For finite r>=0, (ofReal(r))^u=ofReal(r^u); also (ofReal(r^u))*ofReal(r)=ofReal(r^(u+1)).

R102.fact: Multiplication by a fixed nonnegative extended scalar preserves inequalities (with 0*infinity=0). For sequences a_i<=b_i in [0,infinity], sum_i a_i<=sum_i b_i, without finiteness assumptions.

grounds.reason: F003 bounds volume(J_i) by ofReal(rho_i).
The displayed chain multiplies measure inequalities by nonnegative ofReal(rho_i^s) and then sums.

Compare each finite partial sum termwise, then take the supremum over finite index sets, which defines the nonnegative extended sum.

R102.fact: In [0,infinity], if c<=k for every member k of a family K, then c<=inf K, including K empty with inf K=infinity. If f(delta)<=g(delta) for every delta>0, then sup_{delta>0} f(delta)<=sup_{delta>0} g(delta), including infinite suprema.

grounds.reason: F005 makes C_s(delta,A) a lower bound for every admissible product-cover cost.
N101 identifies these infima with the positive-exponent contents and identifies the scale suprema with H.
The scale inequality has been proved for arbitrary positive delta and s+1 is positive.

R102.justification: An infimum is the greatest lower bound, so every lower bound is below it; for an empty family this says only c<=infinity. Each f(delta) is below the supremum of g, making that supremum an upper bound for all f(delta); the least-upper-bound property yields the stated supremum inequality. No interchange of infimum, supremum or integral is involved.

R103.fact: For 0<a≤1, the natural ceiling N=ceil(1/a) is finite and satisfies N≥1, 1/N≤a and N≤1/a+1≤2/a. The N closed intervals [j/N,(j+1)/N], 0≤j<N, cover [0,1] and have diameter 1/N.

grounds.reason: F001 supplies 0<a_i≤r for the chosen budgets.
r=min(1,δ), with δ>0, gives r≤1.

R103.justification: The Archimedean property of the reals gives the least natural integer N≥1/a; its minimality gives N<1/a+1. Positivity permits reciprocation to obtain 1/N≤a. Adjacent interval endpoints agree, their first endpoint is zero and last is one, so their finite union is [0,1]. Distances in each interval are at most its endpoint difference, attained by its endpoints.

R103.fact: If ediam U≤ofReal a with finite a≥0 and J is a real interval of length b≤a, then ediam(U×J)≤ofReal a in MaxProd X. This also holds when U is empty.

grounds.reason: The selected pair supplies ediam U_i≤ofReal a_i and a_i>0.
The constructed intervals have length 1/N_i≤a_i.
Extended diameter is the supremum of pairwise extended distances.
The product distance is the maximum of the two component distances.

R103.justification: Every pair from U has distance ≤a by the diameter bound and the order-preserving embedding of nonnegative finite reals. Every pair from J has distance ≤b≤a. Hence each product distance, their maximum, is ≤a, and taking its supremum preserves the upper bound. An empty product has diameter zero.

R103.fact: For p>0 the extended nonnegative power x↦x^p is increasing. For finite a>0, (ofReal a)^p=ofReal(a^p), and for q>0 one has a^(q+1)=a*a^q. Consequently, N finite product sets each of diameter ≤ofReal a have total p-cost ≤ofReal(N*a^p), including empty sets when p>0.

grounds.reason: L1 gives q>0; thus p=q+1>0.
The chosen budgets are strictly positive finite reals.
The product diameter bounds and finite positive integers N_i have been established.
Real powers use exp(p log a) on positive bases and zero at base zero for positive exponents.

R103.justification: Monotonicity of log and exp proves power monotonicity for positive finite bases; the specified zero and infinity values give the endpoints. The exponential addition law gives a^(q+1)=a*a^q. Embedding nonnegative finite values commutes with these powers and finite sums. Bounding each of N costs and summing gives the stated inequality; empty-set cost is zero.

R103.fact: For finite natural N_i≥1, the set T={(i,j):i∈ℕ,j<N_i} has a natural enumeration without repetitions. For nonnegative extended costs c_(i,j), enumeration preserves the total sum and Σ_T c=Σ_i Σ_(j<N_i)c_(i,j). Nonnegative sums preserve termwise inequalities and commute with multiplication by a finite positive constant, in particular 2.

grounds.reason: Each N_i is a finite positive natural; all product costs and comparison terms lie in [0,∞].
Cover costs are nonnegative extended sums over natural indices.

R103.justification: List pairs in successive finite diagonals of ℕ×ℕ and retain exactly those in T. Every admissible pair occurs once; the pairs (i,0) show that the retained list is infinite. A nonnegative sum is the supremum of its finite subsums, so a bijection preserves it. Every finite set of pairs is contained in finitely many complete finite rows; conversely such rows form a finite set of pairs. This gives the regrouping identity. Termwise comparison follows on finite subsums. Multiplication by a fixed positive finite constant is an order isomorphism of [0,∞], hence preserves their suprema and gives the scaling identity.

R103.fact: If z∈[0,∞] satisfies z≤ofReal(2ε) for every real ε>0, then z=0.

grounds.reason: F002 supplies a cover of cost <ofReal(2ε) for every positive ε at the fixed positive scale.
N101 identifies the relevant content with the infimum of these cover costs.

R103.justification: Choosing ε=1 bounds z by the finite value 2, excluding infinity. If its finite real value t were positive, ε=t/4 would give t≤t/2, a contradiction. Nonnegativity therefore forces z=0. The subsequent supremum is a supremum of zero contents by N101, without any exchange of limits or integrals.

R104.fact: For a metric space X, d((x,t),(y,u))=max(d_X(x,y),|t−u|) is a finite metric on X×ℝ. The usual real metric and this product metric induce extended metrics, so the supplied extended-metric dimension statements apply to them.

grounds.reason: X is an arbitrary metric space.
D009 specifies exactly this product set and distance; the real factor has its usual metric.

R104.justification: Nonnegativity and symmetry follow from those of each factor. The maximum vanishes exactly when both factor distances vanish, hence exactly when both coordinates coincide. For three points the two factor triangle inequalities and max(a+c,b+d)≤max(a,b)+max(c,d) prove the product triangle inequality. All distances are finite. Embedding a finite nonnegative distance into [0,∞] preserves zero, order and addition, yielding the corresponding extended metric axioms.

R105.fact: For z∈[0,∞] with z≠∞, z.toReal≥0 and ofReal(z.toReal)=z. For nonnegative real a,b, ofReal a≤ofReal b iff a≤b, likewise for strict inequality, and ofReal(a+b)=ofReal a+ofReal b. Every ofReal b is finite; consequently z≤ofReal b implies z≠∞. Also 0≠∞ and ∞≤z implies z=∞.

grounds.reason: D003 defines ofReal as the nonnegative real embedding and toReal as the finite real value, with infinity the added top element.
D007 places dimH in [0,∞].
L1 provides dimH A≠∞, the actual condition for recovering dimH A from D0.

R105.justification: The extended nonnegative reals consist of the nonnegative reals and an added largest element infinity. On finite nonnegative values, the embedding and finite-value map are inverse and the order and addition are the real ones. A finite embedded value is strictly below infinity, so a value bounded by it cannot be infinity. Top-element antisymmetry gives the last implication. These facts justify the initial identification and subsequent finite-value comparisons and addition; S004 establishes product finiteness before applying the finite inverse there.

R105.fact: For any metric space X, the formula d((x,t),(y,u))=max(d_X(x,y),|t−u|) makes X×ℝ a metric space and hence an extended metric space via edist=ofReal d. Equipping it with its own Borel sigma algebra satisfies the Borel-space premises of M004 and M005 without any assumption on the subset G.

grounds.reason: X is an arbitrary metric space with its Borel sigma algebra.
D009 specifies this maximum distance and chooses the Borel sigma algebra for Hausdorff-measure statements.
D002 identifies metric edist with ofReal of distance.

R105.justification: Nonnegativity and symmetry hold in each coordinate; distance zero forces both coordinates equal. Each coordinate distance obeys the triangle inequality and is bounded by the maximum on its corresponding leg, so both coordinate distances across a triangle are bounded by the sum of the two leg maxima; taking their maximum proves the product triangle inequality. Embedding the nonnegative metric distances gives the extended metric inequalities. The sigma algebra generated by this metric's open sets is its Borel structure by construction; no product-sigma-algebra identification or measurability of G is needed.

R106.fact: For a,b,d≥0 with d²=a²+b² and m=max(a,b), one has m≤d≤√2·m. Here √2 is finite nonnegative and (√2)²=2.

grounds.reason: a and b are respectively a Euclidean norm and an absolute value; d is the Euclidean target distance, and the displayed finite-sum computation establishes d²=a²+b².
The norm is the nonnegative square root of the finite sum of coordinate squares.

R106.justification: Since 0≤a,b≤m and m is one of a,b, m²≤a²+b²≤2m²=(√2·m)². Squaring preserves and reflects order between nonnegative reals: if 0≤x<y then y²−x²=(y−x)(y+x)>0. Apply this to the two inequalities. These are exactly the square-root and sign conditions used in S001.

R106.fact: If (Z,d) is a metric space, then d_max((x,t),(y,u))=max(d(x,y),|t−u|) is a metric on Z×ℝ; its finite distances canonically define an extended metric. Thus MaxProd(Ambient n) and Ambient(n+1) satisfy the space hypotheses of M006/M007 for every n≥0.

grounds.reason: Ambient m is the specified Euclidean inner product space with its norm distance, for all natural m including zero.
MaxProd uses exactly the maximum of the given metric distance and real absolute difference.

R106.justification: Nonnegativity and symmetry follow for each component. A zero maximum forces both component distances to vanish, hence equality of both coordinates. Each component distance across three points is at most the sum of the corresponding two component distances, which is at most the sum of the two maxima; taking the maximum proves the triangle inequality. Embedding nonnegative finite distances into [0,∞] preserves these metric axioms. No dimension or nonemptiness condition is introduced.

R107.fact: For finite a,b∈[0,∞], if b=a+1 then b.toReal=a.toReal+1, and a+1 is finite. Here a=dimH(E) and b=dimH(appendCoord(n) '' (E×I)).

grounds.reason: D003 identifies finite extended nonnegative reals with their real values.
N004 supplies finiteness of dimH(E).
N105 supplies finiteness and the dimension equality for the maximum product.

R107.justification: Finite extended nonnegative reals are nonnegative real numbers under the canonical embedding. Their finite sums agree with real addition; the sum of the finite representatives a.toReal and 1 is finite. Applying the inverse real-value identification to b=a+1 gives the stated equality.

source_steps.text: Ambient n is the n-coordinate real inner product space, hence a finite-dimensional real normed vector space: its n coordinate vectors span and are independent, also for the empty coordinate family at n=0. Apply M008 to E⊆univ, M009 to this whole space, and M011 with scalar field ℝ and natural index n. This gives dimH E≤dimH(univ:Ambient n)=finrank(ℝ,Ambient n)=n. Nonnegativity is part of the [0,∞] codomain of dimH. M010 applied to E in the same space gives dimH E≠∞. No compactness or nonemptiness is used.
In the one-dimensional real normed space ℝ, 0≠1 and 0≤1. M012 gives dimH(segment(ℝ,0,1))=1; M013 gives segment(ℝ,0,1)=[0,1]=I. Substitution proves dimH I=1.

Fix arbitrary X,A,s, and assume L1: s>0. For an empty cover member, ediam ∅=0 and 0^s=0, so its guarded cost in Content is zero, exactly the raw diameter-power cost. For a nonempty member the supremum over its nonemptiness witnesses is that same power. Thus C_s is the stated raw countable-cover infimum. If 0<δ₁≤δ₂, each δ₁-cover is a δ₂-cover; taking infima gives C_s(δ₂,A)≤C_s(δ₁,A). Apply M001 at X,A,s. Its positive extended-scale supremum equals the positive finite real-scale supremum: every finite positive real scale is an allowed extended scale, while any h∈(0,∞] admits a finite real δ>0 with ofReal δ≤h (take δ=h.toReal/2 when h<∞, and δ=1 when h=∞). Scale antitonicity then bounds the content at h by the one at δ. This proves the normalization and supremum statements F001. The countable covers here are exactly those in problem.md; finite covers can be padded by empty sets.

Fix arbitrary real r,ε, and assume L2: H^s(A)=0, r>0 and ε>0. F001 and nonnegativity give C_s(r/2,A)=0. The defining infimum then has a cover with cost <ofReal(ε/4): if no admissible cover had cost below that positive number, the infimum would be at least that number. In particular admissible covers exist; otherwise the infimum is ∞. This proves F002.

Choose U from F002, and define d_i=(ediam U_i).toReal and e_i=ε·2^(−i−3). Since ediam U_i≤ofReal(r/2)<∞, we have 0≤d_i≤r/2<r and ediam U_i=ofReal d_i. Therefore the original cost is Σ_i ofReal(d_i^s)<ofReal(ε/4). Each e_i is positive and Σ_i e_i=ε/4: the first m terms sum to (ε/4)(1−2^(−m)), tending to ε/4. These finite partial sums also establish the corresponding extended-nonnegative sum identity.

Use M020 with exponent s≥0. For each natural index i, continuity of x↦x^s at d_i and the strict gap d_i<r from F003 permit a positive η_i smaller than r−d_i and small enough that |(d_i+η_i)^s−d_i^s|<e_i. Indeed the continuity neighborhood for error e_i>0 contains an interval about d_i, and one can take half the minimum of its positive radius and r−d_i. Then d_i+η_i is in (d_i,r) and its s-power is <d_i^s+e_i. Countable choice of these individual values yields the sequence-existence statement F004; no covering sets are enlarged.

Choose a from F004. By F003 and F004, 0<a_i≤r and ediam U_i=ofReal d_i≤ofReal a_i. Comparing nonnegative finite partial sums and then their suprema gives Σ_i ofReal(a_i^s)≤Σ_i ofReal(d_i^s)+Σ_i ofReal(e_i)<ofReal(ε/2)<ofReal ε. Addition of these nonnegative sums is justified by the finite partial-sum identity and taking increasing suprema; all right-hand totals here are finite. This proves the required cover and positive budgets for every r,ε under L2. Discharge L2 into the stated implication, and discharge L1 into the positive-exponent universal statement. Together with F001 this proves all the claimed cover-content and positive-budget statements. Empty cover members received positive numerical budgets in the same way; the proof also works in singleton and zero-dimensional spaces.

Fix arbitrary X,A,s,δ and assume L1: s>0 and δ>0. Fix an arbitrary sequence V and assume L2: V covers A×I and ediam V_i≤ofReal δ for every i. Define ρ_i=(ediam V_i).toReal, Aproj_i=π_X(V_i), Bproj_i=π_ℝ(V_i). All ρ_i lie in [0,δ], and ediam V_i=ofReal ρ_i. The two coordinate projections are 1-Lipschitz, since each coordinate distance is bounded by their maximum, the source distance. Applying M021 to each projection therefore gives ediam Aproj_i≤ofReal ρ_i and ediam Bproj_i≤ofReal ρ_i. For empty V_i both projections and their diameters are empty and zero. This proves F001.

Each Bproj_i is bounded in ℝ. If it is empty this is immediate. Otherwise, for any t_i∈Bproj_i, every t∈Bproj_i satisfies |t−t_i|≤ρ_i by F001 and the defining diameter bound. Thus Bproj_i⊆[t_i−ρ_i,t_i+ρ_i], a bounded interval. This proves the boundedness statement F002 without choosing any measurable projection or any uniform center.

Define J_i=[inf Bproj_i,sup Bproj_i] for nonempty V_i and J_i=∅ for empty V_i. For a nonempty index, M018 and F002 give Bproj_i⊆J_i, M017 gives ediam Bproj_i=ofReal(sup Bproj_i−inf Bproj_i), and M019 gives volume(J_i)=that same quantity≤ofReal ρ_i by F001. For empty indices inclusion and the zero volume bound are immediate. Every J_i is closed (or empty), hence Borel measurable; so is J_i∩I because I is closed. M019 at 0,1 also gives volume(I)=ofReal(1−0)=1. These are F003.

Put c=C_s(δ,A) and W(t)_i=Aproj_i if t∈J_i, otherwise ∅. For each t∈I these sets cover A: for any x∈A, the cover V contains (x,t) in some V_i, hence x∈Aproj_i and t∈Bproj_i⊆J_i by F003. Each W(t)_i has extended diameter≤ofReal δ by F001, and its s-cost is at most ofReal(ρ_i^s)1_{J_i}(t), since s>0. N101's raw infimum formula yields c≤Σ_i ofReal(ρ_i^s)1_{J_i}(t). Define h=c1_I and g_i=ofReal(ρ_i^s)1_{J_i∩I}. On I the preceding inequality gives h≤Σ_i g_i; outside I both sides are zero. All g_i and h are Borel measurable: they take fixed constants on measurable sets and zero elsewhere, also when c=∞. This proves F004; we never require c to be finite.

Integrate the pointwise inequality of F004 with respect to volume on ℝ by M016. Apply M014 to the natural-indexed measurable family g, and M015 to h=c1_I and to each g_i. Using F003 and measure monotonicity gives
c=c·volume(I)=∫⁻h≤∫⁻Σ_i g_i=Σ_i∫⁻g_i
 =Σ_i ofReal(ρ_i^s) volume(J_i∩I)
 ≤Σ_i ofReal(ρ_i^s) volume(J_i)
 ≤Σ_i ofReal(ρ_i^s) ofReal ρ_i
 =Σ_i ofReal(ρ_i^(s+1))=Σ_i(ediam V_i)^(s+1).
For ρ_i>0 the last power identity is ρ_i^s·ρ_i=ρ_i^(s+1); for ρ_i=0 both s and s+1 are positive so both sides are zero. Empty indices also contribute zero. Measure monotonicity needs no additional measurability condition. Nonnegative sums are compared by finite partial sums and their suprema. These operations hold in [0,∞], with 0·∞=0 as usual; c·1=c even for c=∞. Since V was arbitrary, discharge L2 and universally quantify V. This is F005.

Take the infimum of the cover costs in F005. N101 applies to exponent s+1>0 and gives C_s(δ,A)≤C_{s+1}(δ,A×I). This infimum argument is valid even if no δ-cover exists, in which case its right-hand infimum is ∞. The argument holds for every real δ>0. Take the supremum over these scales, and use N101 for both spaces and positive exponents s and s+1, to obtain H^s(A)≤H^{s+1}(A×I). Discharge L1 and universally quantify X,A,s,δ. This proves the slicing inequality with constant one, for arbitrary subsets and without compactness.

Fix X,A,q, and assume L1: q>0 and H^q(A)=0. Fix arbitrary real δ,ε and assume L2: δ>0 and ε>0. Define r=min(1,δ)>0. N101, instantiated with s=q and this r,ε, gives existence of a pair consisting of a cover U of A and budgets a_i with 0<a_i≤r, ediam U_i≤ofReal a_i and Σ_i ofReal(a_i^q)<ofReal ε. Record this as F001 before choosing the pair.

Choose the pair (U,a) from F001. Define N_i=ceil(1/a_i). Since 0<a_i≤r≤1, N_i≥1, 1/N_i≤a_i and N_i≤1/a_i+1≤2/a_i. Partition I by the N_i closed intervals Jpart_(i,j)=[j/N_i,(j+1)/N_i] for 0≤j<N_i. The products Ppart_(i,j)=U_i×Jpart_(i,j) cover A×I. Distances within each product are bounded by max(a_i,1/N_i)≤a_i, so its extended diameter is ≤ofReal a_i≤ofReal δ. Their index set {(i,j): i∈ℕ,0≤j<N_i} injects into ℕ×ℕ, which is enumerated by successive finite diagonals. Thus the products can be reindexed as a natural sequence, with empty padding if necessary. Reindexing preserves the sum of nonnegative costs: both are suprema of the same finite subfamily sums. Their total (q+1)-cost satisfies
Σ_i Σ_{j<N_i}(ediam Ppart_(i,j))^(q+1)
 ≤Σ_i ofReal(N_i a_i^(q+1))
 ≤Σ_i ofReal((2/a_i)a_i^(q+1))
 =2Σ_i ofReal(a_i^q)<ofReal(2ε).
All divisions are by positive a_i; real powers give a_i^(q+1)/a_i=a_i^q. This proves the countable-cover existence and cost bound F002, with absolute constant 2.

N101 identifies C_{q+1}(δ,A×I) with the cover-cost infimum. By F002 it is ≤ofReal(2ε) for every ε>0 at each fixed δ>0, so it is zero: any positive finite lower bound is contradicted by taking a smaller ε, and even one such finite bound excludes ∞. Discharge L2 to obtain the asserted existence for every δ,ε>0 and zero content for every δ>0. N101's finite-positive-scale supremum then yields H^{q+1}(A×I)=0. Discharge L1 and universally quantify X,A,q. This proves both claimed clauses, including the scale/tolerance statement and its constant.
Fix X,A and assume L1: A is nonempty. This says precisely that there exists a point x₀∈A, the existence recorded as F001.

Choose x₀∈A from F001 and define f:ℝ→MaxProd X by f(t)=(x₀,t). For all real t,u, d_max(f(t),f(u))=max(d_X(x₀,x₀),|t−u|)=max(0,|t−u|)=|t−u|. Thus f is both 1-Lipschitz and 1-antilipschitz. Also f '' I⊆A×I, because x₀∈A. Record these facts as F002.

Apply M006 and M007 to f and I using F002; their two opposite image inequalities give dimH(f '' I)=dimH I. N005 says dimH I=1. Apply M008 in MaxProd X to the inclusion in F002, obtaining 1=dimH(f '' I)≤dimH(A×I). Discharge L1 and quantify X,A. This proves the claimed lower bound; the chosen point's identity is absent from the conclusion.

Fix X,A and assume L1: A is nonempty and dimH A≠∞. Define D0=(dimH A).toReal and G=A×I. Since dimH A is finite and nonnegative, D0≥0 and ofReal D0=dimH A. This establishes F001 and legitimately permits approximation by real exponents.

Fix an arbitrary real q and assume L2: q>D0. Then q>0 by F001. Instantiate M003 with subset A and nonnegative exponent q: ofReal q>dimH A, so H^q(A)=0. N103 with X,A,q yields H^{q+1}(G)=0. Record this exact measure conclusion as F002.

Apply M004 in MaxProd X to G and exponent q+1>0, using F002's zero measure (zero≠∞). It gives dimH G≤ofReal(q+1). Since q was arbitrary, discharge L2 into the complete universally quantified assertion F003.

Take q0=D0+1 in F003; the resulting finite upper bound proves dimH G≠∞. Define T0=(dimH G).toReal, so T0≥0 and ofReal T0=dimH G. To prove the sharp upper bound, assume L3: T0>D0+1, and define qmid=D0+(T0−D0−1)/2. Then qmid>D0 and qmid+1<T0. F003 at qmid gives T0≤qmid+1, a contradiction. Discharge L3 by classical contradiction, obtaining T0≤D0+1. Independently, N104 applies to the nonempty A from F001 and gives dimH G≥1, hence T0≥1. These finite-dimension and bound facts are F004.
Fix an arbitrary real s and assume L4: 0<s<D0. By F001, ofReal s<dimH A. M002 at subset A and nonnegative exponent s gives H^s(A)=∞, the exact assertion F005.
Instantiate N102 with X,A,s. Since s>0, F005 and its measure inequality give ∞=H^s(A)≤H^{s+1}(A×I)=H^{s+1}(G), so H^{s+1}(G)=∞. This is F006.
Apply M005 in MaxProd X at subset G and exponent s+1, using F006. It gives ofReal(s+1)≤dimH G, hence s+1≤T0 by F004. Discharge L4 and quantify the arbitrary s to obtain F007.

By D0≥0 from F001, the cases D0=0 and D0>0 are exhaustive. In the first branch assume L5: D0=0. F004 gives T0≥1=D0+1; close this branch and discharge L5. In the second branch assume L6: D0>0. To prove T0≥D0+1 assume L7: T0<D0+1 and define smid=(max(0,T0−1)+D0)/2. Both 0 and T0−1 are <D0, so max(0,T0−1)<smid<D0. In particular smid>0 and T0<smid+1, whereas F007 gives smid+1≤T0. This is a contradiction; discharge L7, obtaining T0≥D0+1 in this branch, and discharge L6. Case elimination therefore gives T0≥D0+1 universally. With F004's opposite bound, T0=D0+1. Since ofReal D0=dimH A and ofReal T0=dimH G, this is dimH(A×I)=dimH A+1 in [0,∞]. The finiteness clause is F004. Discharge L1 and quantify X,A; this proves the claimed dimension equality and finiteness, including the case D0=0.

The map appendCoord(n) places the n coordinates of its first component before its real second component. Its inverse reads off these first n coordinates and the last coordinate. These coordinate operations are inverse in both orders, so the map is bijective. Fix arbitrary source points p,p′ and put a=‖p.1−p′.1‖₂≥0, b=|p.2−p′.2|≥0. Splitting the finite sum of squares into the first n terms and the last term gives
 d₂(appendCoord(n)p,appendCoord(n)p′)^2
   =Σ_{i<n}|p.1_i−p′.1_i|²+|p.2−p′.2|²=a²+b².
Since max(a,b)²≤a²+b²≤2max(a,b)², taking nonnegative square roots gives
 d_max(p,p′)≤d₂(appendCoord(n)p,appendCoord(n)p′)≤√2·d_max(p,p′).
The maximum is exactly the source distance. Quantifying p,p′, these inequalities establish √2-Lipschitz and 1-antilipschitz bounds. When n=0, the coordinate sum is empty and zero, the first component is the unique vector of Ambient 0, and the same inverse and estimates still apply. Record the full construction and bounds as F001.

Fix an arbitrary subset S⊆MaxProd(Ambient n). Apply M006 with map appendCoord(n) and K=√2≥0, using F001, to obtain dimH(appendCoord(n) '' S)≤dimH S. Apply M007 with the same map and L=1, again using F001, to obtain the reverse inequality. Antisymmetry gives equality for every S. Together with F001's bijectivity and the two explicit distance bounds, this proves the claimed metric bridge and dimension preservation. Both constants are absolute; no norm-invariance assertion is assumed.

Return to the original natural n and E⊆Ambient n. H001 gives that E is nonempty. N004 gives dimH E≤n and dimH E≠∞, including n=0. Instantiate N105 with X=Ambient n and A=E. Its nonemptiness and finite-dimension conditions are exactly these two available facts. It yields dimH(E×I)=dimH E+1 in MaxProd(Ambient n), and finiteness of that product dimension. Now apply N106 to the subset E×I. Under the fixed coordinate identification, appendCoord(n) '' (E×I) is precisely the original E×[0,1] in Euclidean ℝ^(n+1): its first n coordinates belong to E and its last coordinate belongs to [0,1], and conversely every such vector has this preimage. N106 transfers the maximum-metric dimension to this Euclidean image. Therefore dimH(E×[0,1])=dimH E+1 with the stipulated Euclidean metric. Both sides are finite by N004 and N105, so their [0,∞] equality is the equality of finite real dimensions as well. This proves P. The original compactness hypothesis remains retained but is unused in this strengthened basis route.

header:
import Mathlib
open scoped ENNReal NNReal Topology
open MeasureTheory MeasureTheory.Measure Set Metric
namespace YuiBasis
noncomputable def Content {X : Type*} [EMetricSpace X]
    (s : ℝ) (δ : ℝ≥0∞) (A : Set X) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ⨅ (U : ℕ → Set X) (_ : A ⊆ ⋃ i, U i) (_ : ∀ i, Metric.ediam (U i) ≤ δ),
    ∑' i, ⨆ (_ : (U i).Nonempty), Metric.ediam (U i) ^ s
abbrev Ambient (n : ℕ) := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)
def unitInterval : Set ℝ := Set.Icc 0 1
noncomputable def appendCoord (n : ℕ) (p : Ambient n × ℝ) : Ambient (n + 1) :=
  WithLp.toLp 2 (Fin.lastCases p.2 (fun i => p.1 i))
end YuiBasis

open YuiBasis
namespace YuiPlan
noncomputable def H {X : Type*} [MetricSpace X] (s : ℝ) (A : Set X) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  letI : MeasurableSpace X := borel X
  letI : BorelSpace X := ⟨rfl⟩
  hausdorffMeasure s A
noncomputable def C {X : Type*} [MetricSpace X] (s δ : ℝ) (A : Set X) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  YuiBasis.Content s (ENNReal.ofReal δ) A
end YuiPlan
open YuiPlan

premises.statement: E is compact in the Euclidean space Ambient n=ℝ^n.

P.explanation: The public parameters n:ℕ (including zero) and E:Set(EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)) range over exactly the original Euclidean spaces and arbitrary subsets; E.Nonempty and IsCompact E preserve both original hypotheses. unitInterval=Icc 0 1. Fin.lastCases concatenates the n coordinates and final real coordinate, so appendCoord n '' (E×ˢunitInterval) is exactly the original subset E×[0,1] of Euclidean ℝ^(n+1), in both directions by reading those coordinates. The target states its Hausdorff dimension equals dimH E+1 and explicitly asserts both dimensions are finite. dimH is Mathlib's [0,∞]-valued critical-exponent dimension for the same unnormalized Hausdorff construction; for finite values the ENNReal equality is equivalent in both directions to the real-dimension equality. Compactness is retained even though the accepted basis proof does not use it. No n>0, measurability, positive dimension or further regularity premise is added.

conclusion.statement: With the stipulated Euclidean metrics and identification ℝ^n×ℝ=ℝ^(n+1), dimH(E×[0,1])=dimH(E)+1; equivalently dimH(appendCoord(n) '' (E×I))=dimH(E)+1. Both dimensions are finite, so this is also the equality of their real values.
conclusion.type:
dimH (appendCoord n '' (E ×ˢ unitInterval)) = dimH E + 1 ∧
  dimH E ≠ ⊤ ∧ dimH (appendCoord n '' (E ×ˢ unitInterval)) ≠ ⊤

representation: Keep the exact prepared YuiBasis header as prefix. Ambient n is EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n): Fin n is the coordinate index type, and EuclideanSpace is PiLp 2, so 2 is the norm exponent, not a dimension parameter. Native X×ℝ has the maximum metric (Prod.dist_eq); set products are Set.prod (×ˢ). appendCoord uses Fin.lastCases to put t at Fin.last n and x_i at i.castSucc, with WithLp.toLp 2 selecting the target Euclidean norm. T012/T013 prove the actual metric conversion. H s A is the native unnormalized hausdorffMeasure on the canonical Borel sigma algebra of each metric space, with the BorelSpace equality witnessed definitionally; it adds no regularity assumption. C s δ A is exactly prepared Content s (ENNReal.ofReal δ) A. ENNReal.ofReal embeds max(δ,0), and only positive real scales occur in content assertions. Metric.ediam, infima, suprema, sums, dimensions and costs take values in ℝ≥0∞, retaining ∞; ^ on extended diameters is ENNReal real power, while ^ on real budgets is Real.rpow before ofReal. Positive exponents make empty costs zero. dimH uses Borel Hausdorff measure and nonnegative critical exponents intrinsically. Finite-dimensional and finite-product results imply that the final ENNReal equality is also equality of real dimensions. All H premises and N/P outputs are kept; no E exists here, no M port is needed, and reviewed background notes introduce no assumptions.
